item.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence for Planning Scenario Visualization: A Framework and Benchmark for Controllable Street‐Level Image Synthesis
item.description:
Qian Cao, Hilda Kurtz, Jon Calabria, Robert Alfred Vick, Xiaobai Angela Yao, Gengchen Mai
Transactions in GIS, vol. 30, issue 7
DOI: 10.1111/tgis.70431
ABSTRACT The rapid advancement of Generative AI (GenAI) creates new opportunities for spatial planning. However, most existing applications focus on macro‐scale overhead perspectives, leaving street‐level visualization constrained by strict physical and spatial fidelity challenges. We introduce a controllable GenAI‐human interactive framework for producing spatially faithful and realistic street‐level imagery that reflects envisioned planning scenarios. Using Large‐scale solar photovoltaic (LSPV) site planning as a test case, it leverages vision‐language models to integrate human inputs (e.g., textual intent, scribbles) and existing status photos, synthesizing photorealistic outcomes. To support systematic evaluation, we constructed a large‐scale street‐view imagery dataset of before‐and‐after solar panel installation across the United States. We comprehensively evaluated 11 model settings covering five open‐sourced diffusion models and one commercial vision foundation model to test fidelity and realism. Our study illustrates how a GenAI‐human interactive pipeline can support visualizing proposed environmental interventions, and offers a benchmark for conditioned GenAI visualization applications.

item.title: Modeling Hospital Visitation Flows Through Distance‐Attractiveness Tradeoffs: Integrating Human Mobility, Hospital Attributes, and Socioeconomic Context
item.description:
Binbin Lin, Lei Zou, Hao Tian, Heng Cai, Yifan Yang, Bing Zhou
Transactions in GIS, vol. 30, issue 7
DOI: 10.1111/tgis.70432
ABSTRACT Hospital visitation reflects a complex destination‐choice process shaped by travel cost, perceived hospital attractiveness, and neighborhood socioeconomic conditions. However, less is known about how these factors jointly structure realized hospital destination choice and how their relationships vary across travel distances and community contexts. This study integrates 4 years (2020–2023) of anonymized mobility data in Houston, TX, USA, with hospital attributes, Google Maps ratings and review counts, and 2023 American Community Survey socioeconomic indicators, including health‐insurance coverage. Five predictive models were evaluated across multiple test‐set proportions using 10 repeated train‐test splits. The heterogeneous graph neural network (HGNN) consistently achieved the strongest predictive performance, while interpretation of the HGNN identified drive time as the dominant predictor and showed that hospital capacity, occupancy, spatial context, online visibility, ratings, and community characteristics jointly modify visitation patterns. Controlled scenario analyses indicated that rating‐related distance‐decay crossovers vary across socioeconomic contexts rather than following a uniform threshold. These findings highlight hospital visitation as a heterogeneous travel behavior shaped by interacting spatial, institutional, and socioeconomic factors.
